lesson.subject: numeracy
lesson.title: Reading Graphs and Drawing Conclusions
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 3, Session 4
lesson.fileName: Session 4 - Reading Graphs and Drawing Conclusions.pptx

plan.curriculum: Mathematics 2.0, Statistics, Years 5 and 6 (VC2M5ST03, VC2M6ST03): interpret data and communicate findings in the context of the investigation, with conclusions supported by the evidence
plan.shape: problem-first: a misleading graph opens the session so students feel the trap, then the teacher models reading the scale and writing a conclusion
plan.criticalFeature: read the scale before you compare, and only claim what the data shows
decisionPoints: the choice check: which graph shows the data fairly?
the hinge: how much did the score really go up?
plan.anchor: ask, collect, show, tell: every investigation starts with a fair question and ends with what the data shows
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 3? Show the display table (column, dot plot, line) and point out the title, labels and scale on one graph.

studentTools: A ruler for every student, for reading graphs
Printed Worksheet for every student; Extension and Supported Worksheet as needed
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
boardSetup: The week's anchor on the board: ask, collect, show, tell
A sentence frame: The data shows ___ because ___.

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn. Read a column graph and a dot plot, sort supported conclusions, and catch a misleading graph.
resources.title: Reading Graphs and Drawing Conclusions
resources.subtitle: Read the scale first. Only claim what the data shows.

example.prompt: How many lunches were sold on Monday and Tuesday together?

items.prompt: Use the dot plot. Each dot is one family.
The canteen plans to sell 250 lunches next week. Does this week's data make that likely? Explain with numbers.
items.answer: Not likely: only 190 were sold this week, so 250 would need 60 more than this week.

example.prompt: Is 'Friday sold more than Wednesday' supported?

items.prompt: Use the canteen graph. Sort each conclusion.
cards: Every school sells most on Thursday

not supported: Every school sells most on Thursday

example.prompt: Scale starts at 40. A scored 42, B 48. How many more did B score?

items.prompt: Ella read this graph. Find her mistake and fix it.
work: Blue's column is four times as tall,
so Blue got four times as many votes as Red.
items.answer: The scale starts at 70. Red got 72 and Blue got 78, so Blue got only 6 more votes.

items.prompt: Which change would make Ella's graph fair?
items.explain: Starting at 0 makes each column's height match its value, so the columns compare fairly.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option. Comparing two classes, judging two graphs of the same data, and making a misleading graph on purpose, with worked examples.
resources.title: Extension: Data Detectives
resources.subtitle: Compare carefully. Explain the trick.

example.prompt: Write a conclusion comparing 6A and 6B on walking.

items.prompt: Use the double column graph of how 6A and 6B get to school.

parts.prompt: Which way did both classes use equally?
How many more 6B students came by bus?
How many students are in each class?

items.prompt: Write two conclusions about the two classes. Use numbers as evidence in each.
items.answer: For example: More 6B students come by car (12) than 6A (10). 6A has 5 more walkers than 6B.

example.prompt: Two graphs show the same data. How can you tell which is fair?
steps: A fair column graph starts at 0.
example.answer: the one that starts at 0 with equal steps

items.prompt: Graph A: the scale starts at 0. Graph B: the scale starts at 90. Both show test scores of 92 and 96. Which graph would a student use to show off? Why?
items.answer: Graph B: starting at 90 makes a 4-mark rise look huge.

items.prompt: A newspaper graph has no scale at all. Why is that a problem?
items.answer: Without a scale you cannot read the values, so you cannot check any claim.

example.prompt: How could you make 51 and 54 look very different?
steps: Now the columns are 1 and 4 squares tall.
example.answer: start the scale near the values

items.prompt: Make a misleading graph on purpose with data of your own. Then explain the trick, and draw the fair version beside it.
items.answer: Check: the misleading graph uses a trick (scale not at 0, uneven steps or missing labels), the trick is explained, and the fair version starts at 0 with equal steps.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: For students who need more guidance: one question per graph, a ruler routine, and a hint on every question.
resources.title: Reading Graphs: Step by Step
resources.subtitle: Use a ruler. Read the scale first.

example.prompt: How many lunches were sold on Tuesday?
steps: Put a ruler across the top of the Tuesday column.
Read the number on the scale: 45.

items.prompt: How many lunches were sold on Friday?
items.hint: Lay your ruler across the top of the Friday column.

items.prompt: How many more on Thursday than Friday?
items.hint: Read both, then take the smaller from the bigger.

example.prompt: 'Monday sold the most.' True or false?

items.prompt: 'Wednesday sold the fewest lunches (25).' True or false?
'This graph shows what every school sells.' True or false?
items.hint: This data is from one school only.

slides.notes: Session 4 of our statistics week: today we read graphs carefully and tell what the data shows.

Before you start, put boards, markers and a ruler on every desk, and write the sentence frame on the board. Print the Worksheet for everyone, and a few copies of the Extension and the Supported Worksheet.

beats: SAY: Let's warm up with coordinates, fractions and angles.
ASK: How did the point move from 2, 5 to 6, 1?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 4 right, 4 down
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> compare the first numbers, then the second numbers, together. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: 4 right, from 2 to 6, and 4 down,
from 5 to 1. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 4 right, 4 up.
Fix: ask whether 1 is higher or lower than 5, and they fix it.
notes.prep: Review of Week 2 coordinates (the request named the focus). Keep the review under 6 minutes.

beats: ASK: Which is larger: 0.45 or two fifths?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 0.45
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> turn 2/5 into hundredths, 40 hundredths, then compare. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Two fifths is 0.40, so 0.45 is larger. Tick it or fix it.
trap: choosing 2/5 because 5 is bigger than 4.
Fix: write both as hundredths, and they compare again.
notes.prep: Term 3 review: comparing fractions and decimals.

slides.title: Complementary angles
prompts: Two complementary angles: one is 28°. Find the other.

beats: ASK: If two complementary angles are 28 degrees and x, how big is x?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 62
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then on to Fluency.
Less -> draw a right angle split in two, say 90, then subtract. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Complementary angles make 90, and 90 take away 28 is 62.
Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 152, from 180.
Fix: say complementary means 90, and they redo it.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 3 digits

beats: SAY: Now for some written subtraction.
Line up the places, and always start with the ones.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
30 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 315
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 315.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.
notes.prep: Subtraction fluency: 3 digits, then 4, then 5. Keep the whole block under 6 minutes.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 4 digits

beats: SAY: Now it's 4 digits.
It's the same method, just one more column.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 4 713
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 4 713.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.

slides.title: Subtract with the written method: 5 digits

beats: SAY: Now it's 5 digits.
It's the same method, just one more column.
ASK: Use the written method to solve this one.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 34 322
SCAN boards for the regrouped columns.
80%+ -> reveal, then the learning intention.
Less -> model the first column together on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: The answer is 34 322.
Tick it or fix it, and check every step.
trap: taking the smaller digit from the bigger one in every column.
Fix: ask "Is the top digit big enough?", and they regroup and redo it.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to read data displays and write conclusions the data supports.
successCriteria: I can read values from a graph.
I can write a conclusion that the data supports, with a number as evidence.
I can spot a misleading graph and explain why it misleads.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: We've asked, collected and shown our data.
Today is the last step: telling what it shows.
SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: The first one is where we start,
and the second one is our big goal today.
notes.prep: SC1 reading values is reachable for everyone; SC2 a supported conclusion is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 spotting a misleading graph is the stretch.

slides.title: Did Shop B sell lots more?
slides.prompt: Did Shop B sell a lot more than Shop A?

notes.answer: No: only 3 more, the scale starts at 50
beats: POINT to the two columns.
SAY: Here are two shops' ice-cream sales. Shop B's column looks much taller.
ASK: Did Shop B sell a lot more ice-creams than Shop A?
Thumbs up for yes, down for no.
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: many thumbs up
POINT to the scale, starting at 50.
SAY: Now look at the scale. It starts at 50, not 0.
Shop A sold 52 and Shop B sold 55: only 3 more.
SAY: The graph tricked our eyes.
Today we learn to read the scale first,
and only claim what the data really shows.
trap: reading the column heights, not the scale.
Fix: run a finger up the scale from 50, and they read the values.
notes.prep: Problem-first: students feel the trap before the I Do. Under 4 minutes.

slides.meaning: What the data shows, said in a sentence with evidence.
slides.example: Soccer is the most popular: 15 students chose it.

notes.answer: what the data shows, with evidence
beats: POINT to the word.
SAY: This word is conclusion. Say it with me: con-clu-sion.
SAY: A conclusion says what the data shows,
and it gives a number from the data as evidence.
ASK: Does a conclusion need evidence? Thumbs up or down.
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up
trap: giving an opinion as a conclusion.
Fix: ask which number proves it, and they rewrite it.
notes.prep: Conclusion plus evidence is the SC2 habit.

slides.title: Write a conclusion
steps: Find what stands out: biggest, smallest, a difference.
Write a sentence with a number as evidence.
Check: does the data really show it?

answers: Pasta is most popular: 12 students chose it

beats: MODEL reading each column with a ruler.
SAY: Let me read the values: pasta 12, wraps 7, sushi 9, soup 4.
MODEL writing the conclusion.
SAY: Pasta stands out as the biggest, so my conclusion is:
Pasta is the most popular lunch, because 12 students chose it.
ASK: How many more students chose pasta than soup?
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 8
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: 8 more. That's another conclusion with evidence:
8 more students chose pasta than soup.
trap: writing 'pasta is yummy' as a conclusion.
Fix: ask which number proves it, and they rewrite it.
notes.stretch: Write a conclusion about the two middle columns.
notes.help: Use the frame: The data shows ___ because ___.
notes.prep: A conclusion is a claim plus a number from the data. SC2.

slides.title: Spot a misleading graph
steps: Read the scale first: it starts at 40.
A fair column graph starts at 0.

beats: POINT to the columns.
SAY: Team B's column looks four times taller. But I always read the scale first.
POINT to 40 at the bottom of the scale.
SAY: This scale starts at 40, not 0.
So Team A scored 42 and Team B scored 48.
ASK: How many more goals did Team B really score?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 6
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Only 6 more. Starting the scale at 40 makes a small difference look huge.
That's a misleading graph.
trap: saying four times as many.
Fix: read both values from the scale, and they redo the difference.
notes.stretch: Sketch how the fair graph would look.
notes.help: Put a finger on the bottom number of the scale before reading.
notes.prep: Read the scale before comparing: the critical feature. SC3.

slides.title: Which graph shows the data fairly?
slides.prompt: Bike 20, Scooter 25. Point to A, B or C

options.misconception: trusts column heights without checking the scale starts at 0
checks the scale but not the values: bike and scooter are swapped

beats: SAY: Bike got 20 and scooter got 25.
Check each graph's scale and values.
ASK: Which graph shows the data fairly?
20 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then cold call one student: What is wrong with A?
Less -> read the bottom of each scale aloud together. Re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: It's B. Its scale starts at 0, and the values match.
A starts at 15, and C has the values swapped.
trap: pointing to A.
Fix: ask where A's scale starts, and they choose again.
notes.prep: First decision point. A means the scale was not checked; C means values were not read.

slides.title: True or false?
slides.ask: Is the statement true or false? Write T or F.
slides.pivot: read each value with a ruler, then check the statement
slides.followUp: cold call one board: Which numbers prove it?

items.label: Footy is twice as popular as cricket.
Netball has 3 more votes than footy.
Every student in Australia likes soccer best.
items.answer: F: the data is only from our class
items.say: False. This data is only from one class, not all of Australia.

say: Let's check some statements against the graph.
Write T or F on your board.
trap: agreeing with a claim the data cannot show.
Fix: ask who was surveyed, and they rethink it.
notes.stretch: Rewrite each false statement so it is true.
notes.help: Write the five values on your board first.
notes.prep: Guided practice: true and false claims, then one beyond the data. SC2.

slides.title: How much did the score go up?

beats: SAY: This one is just for you.
Read the scale before you answer.
ASK: How much did the spelling score go up from Term 1 to Term 2?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 4
SCAN every board, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then Your turn.
Less -> read the bottom of the scale aloud, then both values. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It went up 4, from 92 to 96.
The scale starts at 90, so the columns exaggerate it. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 'it tripled'.
Fix: read both values from the scale, and they redo it.
notes.prep: The hinge before independent work. Anyone writing 'a lot' or 'triple' starts on the Supported Worksheet with the teacher.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.task: Read graphs, sort conclusions and catch a misleading graph on your worksheet.

beats: POINT to the steps.
SAY: Read each question carefully, solve it carefully, then check your answers.
SAY: If you finish, the Extension is your early finisher option.
Let's read the steps together. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE and ask: Where does this graph's scale start?
TIME: 20 minutes. Stop everyone once at 10 minutes to share a strategy.
trap: a conclusion with no number.
Fix: ask which number proves it, and they add it.
notes.stretch: Extension: comparing two classes, two graphs of one set of data, and a trick graph.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: one question per graph, a ruler routine and hints.
notes.prep: Independent practice: reading, supported conclusions and misleading graphs. The sheet is evidence for SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Write one conclusion this graph supports. Use a number as evidence.

beats: SAY: Here's the last one. Work it out on your own board.
ASK: What is one conclusion this graph supports, with a number as evidence?
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: Tuesday was busiest: 20 books
RECORD who writes a claim with no number, or one the data cannot show.
They start next week's statistics review with the teacher.
trap: writing 'students like Tuesday'.
Fix: none now. Record the name for tomorrow.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2: a new graph, a conclusion with evidence.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner the two checks before you trust a graph.

notes.answer: open - listen for read the scale, and only claim what the data shows
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can write a conclusion the data supports?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit board.
A thumb up with no number in the exit conclusion matters most.
ASK: What two checks do you make before you trust a graph?
20 sec. Cue: Partner B first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
EXPECT: read the scale, and only claim what the data shows
notes.prep: Week close: read the self-assessment beside the exit evidence for next week's review.
